title: Κορυδαλός
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 169 (= Perry 251). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κορυδαλὸς εἰς πάγην ἁλοὺς θρηνῶν ἔλεγεν· « Οἴμοι τῷ ταλαιπώρῳ καὶ δυστήνῳ πτηνῷ· οὐ χρυσὸν ἐνοσφισάμην τινός, οὐκ ἄργυρον, οὐκ ἄλλο τι τῶν τιμίων· κόκκος δὲ σίτου μικρὸς τὸν θάνατόν μοι προὐξένησεν. »
sentences.tr: Korydalos eis pagēn halous thrēnōn elegen· « Oimoi tōi talaipōrōi kai dystēnōi ptēnōi· ou chryson enosphisamēn tinos, ouk argyron, ouk allo ti tōn timiōn· kokkos de sitou mikros ton thanaton moi prouxenēsen. »
sentences.l: A lark, caught in a snare, lamenting was saying: « Alas for me, the wretched and luckless bird; I stole no gold from anyone, nor silver, nor any other of the precious things; but a small grain of wheat has procured death for me. »
sentences.i: A lark, taken in a snare, wailed: « Alas for me, wretched and luckless bird; I filched no one's gold, nor silver, nor anything else of value; but a little grain of wheat has brought me my death. »
sentences.n: ἁλούς is the aorist participle of ἁλίσκομαι, "be caught" — a verb that exists only in this passive sense and serves as the passive of αἱρέω. οἴμοι is οἴ + μοι, "ah, for me", and τῷ ταλαιπώρῳ … πτηνῷ stands in apposition to that μοι: the bird laments over itself. νοσφίζομαι takes the accusative of the thing purloined and the genitive of the person robbed, so τινός is "from anyone". προὐξένησεν is προεξένησεν with ο + ε run together into ου; the mark over the υ is a coronis, identical in shape to a smooth breathing, and it signals the join. προξενέω is to bring a thing about for someone, as a patron brings about a favour.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος πρὸς τοὺς διὰ κέρδος εὐτελὲς μέγαν ὑφισταμένους κίνδυνον.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos pros tous dia kerdos euteles megan hyphistamenous kindynon.
sentences.l: The fable is directed at those who for a paltry gain undergo a great danger.
sentences.n: ὑφίσταμαι is literally to stand under a thing, hence to take it on oneself, to undergo. μέγαν … κίνδυνον is split around the participle; separating an adjective from its noun this way is ordinary Greek, and it throws the weight onto μέγαν, set against εὐτελές. The closing has no verb at all — a bare πρός with the accusative names the target and leaves "the fable is aimed" to be heard.
